object.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; gidayū-bushi, voice and shamisen
object.description: The pop star of Meiji Japan. Gidayū-bushi is the chanted narration of the puppet theatre, voice and shamisen telling the story and playing every part; in the 1890s young women took it up as a concert art, musume-gidayū, and became the first mass popular music of modern Japan, with fan clubs, riots and newspaper gossip. Toyotake Roshō of Osaka was the biggest of them. When the Gramophone Company's recording expedition reached Japan in 1906, she was among the first they cut, and this is that disc: the scene at Tsubosaka temple from an 1879 play, in which the blind Sawaichi and his wife are saved by the Kannon. It is one of the oldest recordings of Japanese music that can be heard anywhere.
facts: The 1906-07 Gaisberg expedition made some 270 Japanese recordings, the first large body of them.
Musume-gidayū drew student audiences so fervent that the police treated them as a public-order problem.
The puppet theatre itself, bunraku, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
